studies.title: Lower dorsal striatum activation in association with neuroticism during the acceptance of unfair offers.
studies.abstract: Unfair treatment may evoke more negative emotions in individuals scoring higher on neuroticism, thereby possibly impacting their decision-making in these situations. To investigate the neural basis of social decision-making in these individuals, we examined interpersonal reactions to unfairness in the Ultimatum Game (UG). We measured brain activation with fMRI in 120 participants selected based on their neuroticism score, while they made decisions to accept or reject proposals that were either fair or unfair. The anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex were more activated during the processing of unfair offers, consistent with prior UG studies. Furthermore, we found more activation in parietal and temporal regions for the two most common decisions (fair accept and unfair reject), involving areas related to perceptual decision-making. Conversely, during the decision to accept unfair offers, individuals recruited more frontal regions previously associated with decision-making and the implementation of reappraisal in the UG. High compared to low neurotic individuals did not show differential activation patterns during the proposal of unfair offers; however, they did show lower activation in the right dorsal striatum (putamen) during the acceptance of unfair offers. This brain region has been involved in the formation of stimulus-action-reward associations and motivation/arousal. In conclusion, the findings suggest that both high and low neurotic individuals recruit brain regions signaling social norm violations in response to unfair offers. However, when it comes to decision-making, it seems that neural circuitry related to reward and motivation is altered in individuals scoring higher on neuroticism, when accepting an unfair offer.

studies.title: Parallel Regulation of Memory and Emotion Supports the Suppression of Intrusive Memories.
studies.abstract: Intrusive memories often take the form of distressing images that emerge into a person's awareness, unbidden. A fundamental goal of clinical neuroscience is to understand the mechanisms allowing people to control these memory intrusions and reduce their emotional impact. Mnemonic control engages a right frontoparietal network that interrupts episodic retrieval by modulating hippocampal activity; less is known, however, about how this mechanism contributes to affect regulation. Here we report evidence in humans (males and females) that stopping episodic retrieval to suppress an unpleasant image triggers parallel inhibition of mnemonic and emotional content. Using fMRI, we found that regulation of both mnemonic and emotional content was driven by a shared frontoparietal inhibitory network and was predicted by a common profile of medial temporal lobe downregulation involving the anterior hippocampus and the amygdala. Critically, effective connectivity analysis confirmed that reduced amygdala activity was not merely an indirect consequence of hippocampal suppression; rather, both the hippocampus and the amygdala were targeted by a top-down inhibitory control signal originating from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. This negative coupling was greater when unwanted memories intruded into awareness and needed to be purged. Together, these findings support the broad principle that retrieval suppression is achieved by regulating hippocampal processes in tandem with domain-specific brain regions involved in reinstating specific content, in an activity-dependent fashion.

studies.title: BDNF Methylation and Maternal Brain Activity in a Violence-Related Sample.
studies.abstract: It is known that increased circulating glucocorticoids in the wake of excessive, chronic, repetitive stress increases anxiety and impairs Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) signaling. Recent studies of BDNF gene methylation in relation to maternal care have linked high BDNF methylation levels in the blood of adults to lower quality of received maternal care measured via self-report. Yet the specific mechanisms by which these phenomena occur remain to be established. The present study examines the link between methylation of the BDNF gene promoter region and patterns of neural activity that are associated with maternal response to stressful versus non-stressful child stimuli within a sample that includes mothers with interpersonal violence-related PTSD (IPV-PTSD). 46 mothers underwent fMRI. The contrast of neural activity when watching children-including their own-was then correlated to BDNF methylation. Consistent with the existing literature, the present study found that maternal BDNF methylation was associated with higher levels of maternal anxiety and greater childhood exposure to domestic violence. fMRI results showed a positive correlation of BDNF methylation with maternal brain activity in the anterior cingulate (ACC), and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), regions generally credited with a regulatory function toward brain areas that are generating emotions. Furthermore we found a negative correlation of BDNF methylation with the activity of the right hippocampus. Since our stimuli focus on stressful parenting conditions, these data suggest that the correlation between vmPFC/ACC activity and BDNF methylation may be linked to mothers who are at a disadvantage with respect to emotion regulation when facing stressful parenting situations. Overall, this study provides evidence that epigenetic signatures of stress-related genes can be linked to functional brain regions regulating parenting stress, thus advancing our understanding of mothers at risk for stress-related psychopathology.

studies.title: Neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in generalized anxiety disorder following mindfulness training.
studies.abstract: Mindfulness training aims to impact emotion regulation. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms can be successfully addressed through mindfulness-based interventions. This preliminary study is the first to investigate neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in GAD following mindfulness training. Furthermore, we compared brain activation between GAD patients and healthy participants at baseline. 26 patients with a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis were randomized to an 8-week Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR, N = 15) or a stress management education (SME, N = 11) active control program. 26 healthy participants were included for baseline comparisons. BOLD response was assessed with fMRI during affect labeling of angry and neutral facial expressions. At baseline, GAD patients showed higher amygdala activation than healthy participants in response to neutral, but not angry faces, suggesting that ambiguous stimuli reveal stronger reactivity in GAD patients. In patients, amygdala activation in response to neutral faces decreased following both interventions. BOLD response in ventrolateral prefrontal regions (VLPFC) showed greater increase in MBSR than SME participants. Functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions increased significantly pre- to post-intervention within the MBSR, but not SME group. Both, change in VLPFC activation and amygdala-prefrontal connectivity were correlated with change in Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) scores, suggesting clinical relevance of these changes. Amygdala-prefrontal connectivity turned from negative coupling (typically seen in down-regulation of emotions), to positive coupling; potentially suggesting a unique mechanism of mindfulness. Findings suggest that in GAD, mindfulness training leads to changes in fronto-limbic areas crucial for the regulation of emotion; these changes correspond with reported symptom improvements.

studies.title: Relationships between changes in sustained fronto-striatal connectivity and positive affect in major depression resulting from antidepressant treatment.
studies.abstract: OBJECTIVE Deficits in positive affect and their neural bases have been associated with major depression. However, whether reductions in positive affect result solely from an overall reduction in nucleus accumbens activity and fronto-striatal connectivity or the additional inability to sustain engagement of this network over time is unknown. The authors sought to determine whether treatment-induced changes in the ability to sustain nucleus accumbens activity and fronto-striatal connectivity during the regulation of positive affect are associated with gains in positive affect. METHOD Using fMRI, the authors assessed the ability to sustain activity in reward-related networks when attempting to increase positive emotion during performance of an emotion regulation paradigm in 21 depressed patients before and after 2 months of antidepressant treatment. Over the same interval, 14 healthy comparison subjects underwent scanning as well. RESULTS After 2 months of treatment, self-reported positive affect increased. The patients who demonstrated the largest increases in sustained nucleus accumbens activity over the 2 months were those who demonstrated the largest increases in positive affect. In addition, the patients who demonstrated the largest increases in sustained fronto-striatal connectivity were also those who demonstrated the largest increases in positive affect when controlling for negative affect. None of these associations were observed in healthy comparison subjects. CONCLUSIONS Treatment-induced change in the sustained engagement of fronto-striatal circuitry tracks the experience of positive emotion in daily life. Studies examining reduced positive affect in a variety of psychiatric disorders might benefit from examining the temporal dynamics of brain activity when attempting to understand changes in daily positive affect.

studies.title: Neurobiology of social reward valuation in adults with a history of anorexia nervosa.
studies.abstract: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a disorder characterized by atypical patterns of reward valuation (e.g. positive valuation of hunger). Atypical reward processing may extend into social domains. If so, such findings would be of prognostic significance as impaired social functioning predicts worse outcome. We explore neural circuits implicated in social reward processing in individuals with a history of AN who are weight-restored relative to controls and examine the effects of illness course on the experience of social value.

studies.title: Neural substrates underlying the tendency to accept anger-infused ultimatum offers during dynamic social interactions.
studies.abstract: In managing our way through interpersonal conflict, anger might be crucial in determining whether the dispute escalates to aggressive behaviors or resolves cooperatively. The Ultimatum Game (UG) is a social decision-making paradigm that provides a framework for studying interpersonal conflict over division of monetary resources. Unfair monetary UG-offers elicit anger and while accepting them engages regulatory processes, rejecting them is regarded as an aggressive retribution. Ventro-medial prefrontal-cortex (vmPFC) activity has been shown to relate to idiosyncratic tendencies in accepting unfair offers possibly through its role in emotion regulation. Nevertheless, standard UG paradigms lack fundamental aspects of real-life social interactions in which one reacts to other people in a response contingent fashion. To uncover the neural substrates underlying the tendency to accept anger-infused ultimatum offers during dynamic social interactions, we incorporated on-line verbal negotiations with an obnoxious partner in a repeated-UG during fMRI scanning. We hypothesized that vmPFC activity will differentiate between individuals with high or low monetary gains accumulated throughout the game and reflect a divergence in the associated emotional experience. We found that as individuals gained more money, they reported less anger but also more positive feelings and had slower sympathetic response. In addition, high-gain individuals had increased vmPFC activity, but also decreased brainstem activity, which possibly reflected the locus coeruleus. During the more angering unfair offers, these individuals had increased dorsal-posterior Insula (dpI) activity which functionally coupled to the medial-thalamus (mT). Finally, both vmPFC activity and dpI-mT connectivity contributed to increased gain, possibly by modulating the ongoing subjective emotional experience. These ecologically valid findings point towards a neural mechanism that might nurture pro-social interactions by modulating an individual's dynamic emotional experience.

studies.title: Altered processing of self-related emotional stimuli in mindfulness meditators.
studies.abstract: Mental health benefits of mindfulness techniques are thought to involve changes in self-processing, such as decreased attachment to the self, higher self-compassion and lower emotional reactivity to inner experience. However, self-related emotion processing in regular mindfulness practitioners is not extensively studied. In the current work we investigate differential neural and behavioral correlates of self-criticism and self-praise in 22 mid-to-long-term mindfulness meditators (LTM) compared to 22 matched meditation-naïve participants (MNP). In an fMRI experiment, participants were presented with blocks of individually selected positive (self-praise, SP), negative (self-critical, SC), negative but not-self-critical (NNSC), and general, neutral (NT) adjectives, and reported their affective state after the blocks. On the neural level, both SP and SC yielded more activation in the dorso-medial prefrontal cortex (DMPFC) in LTM compared to MNP. Activation in this region correlated positively with non-react scores of the Five Facets Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) and showed decreased functional connectivity to posterior midline and parietal regions in LTM compared to MNP during both self-related appraisals. Further, we found evidence for emotional reactivity in LTM on the neural level, particularly during SP. On the behavioral level, a mixed effects analysis revealed significantly higher differences in affective ratings after blocks of SC compared to SP in MNP compared to LTM. Differences in DMPFC activation and affective ratings point towards increased awareness, potentially mindful regulation of SC and SP in LTM, while decreased connectivity to other regions of the default mode network could reflect a decreased self-focus in this group. As such, our results illustrate differences in self-related emotional processes in meditators and offer clinically relevant insights into mechanisms of mindful emotion regulation when facing self-criticism and self-praise.

The abstract does not specify whether a separate control group was reported (I3 not demonstrated), but no exclusion criteria are met and information is insufficient to rule inclusion, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study in healthy human participants viewing emotional visual stimuli; examines habitual emotion regulation (expressive suppression), including anticipatory/antecedent processes, and reports task-related brain activation. No exclusion criteria met. Abstract does not clearly state instructed regulation, so full-text review is warranted to confirm details.

Abstract only states the aim to explore neural mechanisms of negative emotion regulation in PTSD and does not report whether this is a task-based fMRI, specifics of the emotion-regulation task, participant/control group details, or task-related activation results. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Insufficient information to confirm I1–I4, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study in human participants examining emotion regulation (implicit attention shift and appraisal) and reporting task-related brain activations; no exclusion criteria met in the abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study examining volitional emotion regulation in veterans with PTSD and reports neural activation results. It does not clearly state whether a separate control group is included, so include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

This is a review paper (not original task-based fMRI data). Abstract describes a review of measures including self-report, behavioral, psychophysiological, and neural studies, without reporting original fMRI task activation results. Therefore it meets exclusion E1 (non-empirical review without original human data). Inclusion criteria I1 and I4 not demonstrated; I2 met in topic but no task-based fMRI data reported; I3 N/A. Recommend exclusion.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (increase/decrease/maintain) of emotional responses to negative pictures in human participants and reports whole-brain BOLD activation results; meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports human BPD participants and reductions in neural activity in amygdala and ACC, indicating task-related brain activation results; however it does not specify a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation paradigm or use of visual stimuli. Inclusion uncertain from abstract alone — include for full-text review.

Study 2 reports task-based fMRI during a reappraisal emotion-regulation task with negative images and reports amygdala activation during regulation. Human adult participants with matched control group are included. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in healthy human participants; reports task-related brain activation (amygdala attenuation and amygdala–prefrontal connectivity). No exclusion criteria met (not a review and not an empathy/perspective-taking study without regulation instructions).

Study is a structural (morphometric) MRI investigation of grey matter in trichotillomania, not a task-based fMRI emotion regulation study. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I2 (no emotion regulation task/viewing with regulation), I4 (no task-related activation results reported).

Abstract does not describe an emotion regulation task or instructed regulation — it assesses dispositional reappraisal during phobic stimulation (I2 not demonstrated). Inclusion met: I1, I3, I4. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study examining implicit emotion regulation in depressed patients and reports activation changes in corticolimbic regions (task-related brain activation). It does not state whether a separate control group is reported, so include for full-text review to verify I3.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI of children using cognitive reappraisal to regulate emotional responses to visual (sad) stimuli, and reports task-related brain activation (PFC, amygdala). No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not an empathy/perspective-taking task without regulation instruction). Recommend full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (up- and down-regulation) using visual stimuli (angry faces) in patients with depression and healthy controls; reports task-related neural activation (amygdala, insula, prefrontal regions). No exclusion criteria met.

Title and abstract state this is an fMRI study of emotion regulation in bipolar disorder type I with human clinical participants. However, the abstract lacks details on whether a task-based regulation paradigm was used vs passive viewing and whether task-related activation results are reported. Include for full-text review to confirm task details and reported activations.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in healthy humans instructed to use cognitive reappraisal (an emotion regulation task) and reports task-related brain activation results (dmPFC response). No exclusion criteria are met. Full-text review warranted to extract activation coordinates and details.

Abstract reports an empirical task-based fMRI study of human healthy participants using cognitive reappraisal to regulate emotional responses to visual stimuli and reports task-related brain activation; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants and reports task-related brain activation/effective connectivity (DCM) results. No exclusion criteria are met; inclusion criteria I1–I4 are satisfied based on the abstract.

Abstract indicates a study of neural activation during emotion regulation in adolescents with and without suicidal ideation, but does not specify stimulus modality (visual) or full task details. Inclusion uncertain from abstract-only evidence, so include for full-text review.

Study reports task-based fMRI of human participants using a reappraisal (detachment-from-threat) emotion-regulation task and presents reappraisal-related brain activation results (shifts in lateral frontal cortex). Meets inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria apparent.

fMRI study examining neural substrates of emotion regulation in women with PMDD; abstract implies a task probing emotion regulation but does not specify stimuli type, regulation instructions, or presence of a control group. Insufficient detail to confirm all inclusion criteria (especially I2 and I4), so include for full-text review.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met / not demonstrated: I2 (participants performing an emotion-regulation task of visual stimuli as required by the review objective). Study uses thermal pain (non-visual) and manipulates perceived control rather than an explicit regulation task for visual emotional stimuli, so it does not address the review objective.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study where MDD participants performed a voluntary emotion regulation strategy (recalling negative autobiographical memories) with BOLD contrasts reported; includes clinical and control groups. No exclusion criteria met. Full text warranted to confirm stimulus modality relative to review objective.

Excluded because the study examined internal self-referential awareness/introspection (no mention of regulating responses to externally presented visual stimuli), which does not meet the review objective. Inclusion met: I1, I3, I4. Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (emotion regulation of responses to visual stimuli or comparable reappraisal of visual stimuli). Exclusion criteria E1/E2 not met.

Task-based fMRI fear conditioning/extinction protocol constitutes a task involving viewing emotional (fear) stimuli (without instructed regulation) and reports task-related brain activation in human participants. Meets I1, I2 (viewing emotional stimuli/adjacent regulation domain), I3, and I4. No exclusion criteria met (not a non-empirical paper, not an empathy/perspective-taking study). Include for full-text review to confirm task details.

Title/abstract indicate a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (an emotion regulation strategy) in human participants (girls at high risk for depression) and report neural activation; thus inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3, and I4 are met. No exclusion criteria are apparent from the abstract. Include for full-text review to extract activation contrasts and details.

Abstract provides insufficient methodological detail to confirm inclusion: it does not state whether task-based fMRI was used, whether participants performed an instructed emotion-regulation task during fMRI, or whether task-related brain activation results are reported. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract. Include for full-text review to assess I1–I4.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study using an affect-labeling emotion-regulation task in human participants (social phobia groups and healthy controls) and reports task-related amygdala and prefrontal activation/connectivity; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in depressed adolescents, reporting task-related brain activation differences; meets inclusion criteria for task-based fMRI, emotion regulation (reappraisal), applicable participant groups (clinical adolescents with control comparison), and reports activation results. No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation), reports task-related brain activation results, and involves human participants. The abstract does not specify stimulus modality (visual vs. other), so include for full-text review to confirm stimuli were visual and meet the meta-analysis objective.

Abstract implies brain imaging with reported activation of emotion-regulation neurocircuits but does not specify whether participants performed an emotion regulation task or whether humans were tested. Insufficient information to confirm all inclusion criteria, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study of human participants performing cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation). Abstract reports task-related brain activation results (amygdala, prefrontal) during regulation. No exclusion criteria met.

This is a task-based fMRI study in humans with generalized social anxiety disorder performing an emotion regulation task (attention regulation of negative self-beliefs) and reporting task-related neural activation results comparing MBSR vs aerobic exercise. It meets inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports comparisons of gambling disorder patients and healthy controls using brain activation measures of emotion regulation, indicating a task-based fMRI investigation of emotion regulation in human participants. Include for full-text review to confirm task specifics and contrasts.

Event-related task-based fMRI with healthy human participants performing a cognitive control task over emotional stimuli (CECT). Reports task-related brain activation (fronto-cingulate, amygdala) and links habitual reappraisal/suppression to performance and activation. Although not an explicit instructed regulation task, the study assesses cognitive control of emotion (allowed). No exclusion criteria met.

Study used diffusion tensor imaging (structural MRI) and self-report measures, not task-based fMRI; participants did not perform an emotion regulation task during scanning and no task-related activation results are reported. Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task), I4 (reports task-related brain activation results).

Abstract reports a task-based rt-fMRI study in humans training emotion regulation using a 'reality check' strategy during presentation of emotional pictures, includes healthy participants and a control group, and reports task-related activation and connectivity (amygdala down-regulation). No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of human participants performing emotion regulation of negative visual stimuli, examining SSRI effects and 5-HTTLPR moderation and reporting neural (fMRI) outcomes. This meets the review’s task, participant, and activation-report criteria. No exclusion criteria are indicated in the abstract.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in adolescent girls with PTSD and reports task-related amygdala functional connectivity changes associated with symptom reduction. This meets inclusion criteria I1–I4 and no exclusion criteria are indicated in the abstract.

No active emotion-regulation task: study measured dispositional cognitive reappraisal and related it to fear conditioning but did not instruct participants to regulate during the fMRI task. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met: I2 (participants performing an emotion regulation task). Exclusion criteria: none met.

Abstract describes an empirical task-based rtfMRI neurofeedback study in healthy human participants targeting hippocampal activation to enhance emotion regulation. Exclusion criteria are not met. However, the abstract does not specify that participants regulated emotional responses to visual stimuli or used explicit emotion-regulation strategies (I2 uncertain). Full-text review needed to confirm relevance to the meta-analysis objective.

Abstract indicates an fMRI task involving observation of risk-taking actions and suggests investigation of emotion-related processing; it is unclear whether participants actively regulated emotions or merely viewed stimuli. Task-based fMRI, human participants, and task-related activation are implied, so include for full-text review to determine presence of regulation instructions.

No task-based emotion regulation paradigm reported: study uses resting-state fMRI examining inflammation and rsFC. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants implied). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I2 (no emotion regulation task), I4 (no task-related activation reported).

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human children (clinical MDD history and controls) and reports task-related functional connectivity results; no exclusion criteria met.

No task-based fMRI or emotion-regulation task: the study is a resting-state fMRI investigation and does not report task-related activation. Exclusion criteria: none met. Inclusion criteria met: none clearly satisfied. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not task-based), I2 (no emotion regulation task/strategy reported), I4 (no task-related activation results), I3 not demonstrated (clinical sample implied but control group not reported).

Title and abstract indicate a task-based fMRI study of emotion regulation in adolescent major depressive disorder, reporting amygdala response and functional connectivity consistent with task-related brain activation. This meets I1–I4. No exclusion criteria are indicated in the abstract. Full-text review warranted to confirm details (e.g., control group reporting).

Study reports task-based fMRI in human participants performing cognitive reappraisal (watch vs reappraise) with clinical (SAD) and healthy control groups, and reports task-related brain activation/connectivity results. No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract describes an empirical task-based fMRI study in humans using cognitive reappraisal to regulate emotion, reports task-related brain activation results, and includes clinical and control groups. No exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in which human participants cognitively up-regulated (engaged) positive-social emotions from a first-person perspective and reports fMRI activation and effective connectivity results. This meets inclusion criteria I1–I4 and does not meet any exclusion criteria. Full text review recommended to extract details.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) during peer-rejection in depressed and non-depressed adolescents and reports functional connectivity/brain activation findings. This meets inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3 and I4 and no exclusion criteria are evident. Include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI with healthy human participants instructed to regulate (expressive suppression) and imitate emotional facial expressions while viewing dynamic visual stimuli; reports task-related brain activation. Meets I1–I4. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in healthy human participants, with voxelwise task-related brain activation results (PFC and amygdala). This satisfies inclusion criteria I1–I4 and no exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in smokers using cognitive reappraisal to regulate craving (emotion regulation). It addresses brain activation (dACC) related to regulation, meeting inclusion for full-text review. The abstract does not explicitly report activation results, so full text is needed to confirm I4.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of human participants performing explicit emotion regulation (up-/downregulation) while viewing negative images, reports task-related brain activation (VLPFC, amygdala), and includes clinical groups and healthy controls. No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study with human participants performing an active cognitive emotion regulation task (cognitive reappraisal), includes both depressed patients and healthy controls, and reports whole-brain activation and connectivity results relevant to regulation vs. passive viewing; meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are met.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI of human participants performing cognitive reappraisal (down-/up-regulation) of visual/episodic negative images, reports task-related brain activation results. No exclusion criteria met.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI not stated in abstract), I2 (no evidence participants performed an emotion-regulation task on visual stimuli—study involves mood induction and pain), I4 (task-related brain activation results not reported in abstract). Therefore excluded from this review.

E1: This paper is a review/meta-analysis and does not present original task-based fMRI data. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (not an original task-based fMRI study), I2 (no original human participants performing an emotion-regulation task), I3 (no participant groups reported as original data), I4 (no original task-related activation results).

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in humans using a cognitive reappraisal emotion-regulation task, reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results, and includes healthy adult participants. All inclusion criteria are met; no exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study (I1) where human participants (adult females) performed emotion regulation tasks (attend, expressive suppression, cognitive reappraisal) to negative images (I2, I3) and presents task-related brain activation and connectivity results (I4). No exclusion criteria are met. Abstract provides sufficient information for inclusion in full-text review.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in adult humans using instructed cognitive reappraisal (Social-Reg) versus look, reporting task-related brain activation contrasts and associations with behavior; meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are evident.

Task-based fMRI with human participants instructed to regulate responses to visual food stimuli using cognitive reappraisal, suppression and up-/down-regulation; reports task-related brain activation results. Fits meta-analysis objective of regulation of emotional/affective responses to visual stimuli.

No emotion regulation instruction reported (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (task-related brain activation results). Exclusion criteria met: none. Therefore excluded because participants viewed stimuli without performing a defined emotion-regulation task required for the review.

Task-based fMRI in human participants comparing emotion-regulation-related instructions (permit/accept vs view) during viewing of unpleasant and neutral visual stimuli; reports subjective ratings and task-related brain activation (amygdala). Meets I1–I4 and no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in adult human participants that reports task-related brain activation (PFC and amygdala). The abstract meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are apparent, so include for full-text review.

Abstract reports neural activity during explicit emotion regulation in humans and links it to resting-state vmHRV, implying a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation study that reports task-related brain activation. Meets inclusion criteria I1-I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Meets inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants (children/adolescents with ASD and TD controls) and reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants; reports task-related brain activation (prefrontal, cingulate, occipital, subcortical) across experiments, meeting inclusion criteria for meta-analysis.

Exclusion E1 applies: this paper is a meta-analysis (no original human data). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI study), I2 (does not involve an emotion regulation task), I3 (no original human participants reported), I4 (does not report original task-related activation results).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) using standardized negative scripts in human participants, with clinical and control groups and task-related brain activation results. All inclusion criteria are met; include for full-text review to confirm stimulus modality (script-driven vs. visual) and extract activation contrasts.

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that directly tests emotion regulation (reappraisal and suppression) while viewing negative pictures and reports neural activation results, satisfying the review objective and inclusion criteria.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using cognitive reappraisal (distancing) in healthy human participants and presents task-related brain activation results (ventral striatum, fronto-parietal network). No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports an empirical task-based fMRI study of an emotion regulation (ER) task in human participants (n=60) and presents task-related neural activation changes pre- to post-training. No exclusion criteria are met.

The study uses recall of an anger-inducing autobiographical memory (no visual stimuli), so it does not address the meta-analysis objective of regulating emotional responses to visual stimuli. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: regulation of emotional responses to visual stimuli (study uses autobiographical recall).

Task-based fMRI with human participants (N=10) performing emotion regulation tasks (reappraisal and affect labeling) and reporting task-related brain activation (amygdala, IFG). Tasks involve regulating emotional responses and fit the meta-analysis objective. No exclusion criteria met.

Study uses auditory stimuli (angry prosody) rather than visual stimuli required by the review objective, so it does not address the review's focus on regulation of visual emotions. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1, I2, I3, I4. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: regulation of visual stimuli (modality requirement).

Abstract reports cognitive reappraisal of palatable food images in human participants across a BMI range and describes modulation of neural responsivity—matching emotion regulation of visual stimuli and task-related brain activation. The abstract does not explicitly state 'task-based fMRI', so include for full-text review to confirm imaging modality.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in which SAD patients performed emotion-regulation tasks (breath-focused and distraction-focused attention) while reacting to negative self-beliefs and shows task-related brain activation changes (amygdala and attentional regions). It is unclear whether stimuli were visual and no control group is mentioned; insufficient information to exclude. Include for full-text review to confirm visual-stimuli requirement and presence/absence of separate control group.

Task-based model-based fMRI in human participants using cognitive emotion regulation (aversive conditioning with and without regulation), reporting prediction error-related and task-related neural activation. No exclusion criteria met.

Human task-based rtfMRI study reporting task-related activation and voluntary modulation of emotional states via neurofeedback. Abstract does not clearly state regulation of responses to visual stimuli or a view condition/comparison common in the review objective, so inclusion is uncertain from abstract alone — include for full-text review.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using a film-based emotion regulation task in human adolescents/young adults and presents task-related neural activation results (prefrontal cortex, amygdala). No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI study of emotion regulation (reappraisal/detachment) with passive viewing; includes clinical (AN) and age-matched control groups; reports behavioral arousal ratings and task-related fMRI activation results—meets all inclusion criteria.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (human clinical and control groups reported). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI study; uses structural MRI/gray matter volume), I2 (participants did not perform an emotion regulation task), I4 (does not report task-related brain activation results). Therefore excluded based on failure to meet required inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I4.

Task-based real-time fMRI neurofeedback study in human adolescents (7–16) teaching up-/down-regulation of an emotion-regulation region (insula); reports task-related activation and connectivity. Unclear whether regulation targeted emotional responses to visual stimuli specifically, but meets broad emotion-regulation criteria and warrants full-text review.

Abstract reports a randomized, placebo-controlled task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in healthy adults and presents task-related activation and functional connectivity results (amygdala and dlPFC). No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract. Full-text review warranted to extract details.

Study reports a task-based fMRI experiment in healthy human (female) participants performing voluntary emotion regulation of emotional pictures and reports task-related brain activation results; matches I1, I2, I3, and I4. No exclusion criteria met.

Patient-only fMRI neurofeedback study (Patients n=10) with no separately reported control group in the abstract. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (participants performed an emotion regulation task—downregulation while viewing trauma words), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criterion not met/not demonstrated: I3 (no control group reported for the patient sample). Exclusion criteria: none met (E1,E2 not applicable).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study including an explicit cognitive emotion regulation task and an emotional Stroop, includes patient and control groups, and reports task-related brain activation (left supramarginal gyrus). No exclusion criteria met. Include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI study (N=26) of primiparous mothers using distraction to regulate emotions in response to infant crying; reports reduced amygdala activation with regulation. Satisfies I1,I2,I3,I4. Stimulus modality appears auditory (infant crying) not visual, so relevance to the visual-stimulus meta-analysis objective is uncertain; include for full-text review.

Excluded because the study uses resting-state fMRI acquired before and after an emotion-regulation task rather than reporting task-based fMRI activation; therefore I1 (task-based fMRI) and I4 (task-related activation results) are not met. It meets I2 (participants performed an emotion regulation task) and I3 (clinical and control groups). No exclusion criteria apply.

Abstract reports a neuroanatomical MRI study of somatoform disorders with no mention of task-based fMRI, emotion regulation tasks, or task-related activation results. Inclusion criteria I1, I2, and I4 are not met; I3 (participant groups) is not demonstrated. No exclusion criteria (E1/E2) apply based on the abstract.

Task-based fMRI in humans comparing emotion regulation strategies (cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression) to natural viewing of visual scenes; reports task-related brain activation results and manipulates stimulus valence and social content. Meets I1, I2, I3, I4; no exclusion criteria apparent.

No emotion-regulation task is reported in the abstract (I2 not met). The study is a task-based human fMRI experiment reporting task-evoked activation (I1 and I4 met). Participant details are not specified in abstract (I3 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria (E1/E2) appear applicable.

Excluded because the study did not use task-based fMRI (I1 not met); it used magnetoencephalography and structural MRI. Inclusion criteria met: I2 (task involving inhibition of aversive socio-emotional stimuli), I3 (human participants—school-age children), I4 (reports task-related functional brain activity). Exclusion criteria met: none.

Abstract describes an fMRI study in adolescents examining brain responses/connectivity to emotional frustration (task-based fMRI, human participants, reports task-related brain activation/connectivity). It does not clearly state whether an explicit emotion-regulation instruction (reappraisal/distancing/etc.) was used, so I2 is uncertain; include for full-text review to verify.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study (I1) using cognitive emotion regulation/reappraisal during reward anticipation (I2) in healthy human participants (I3) and reports task-related brain activation results (DLPFC, putamen, PPI) (I4). No exclusion criteria are met; include for full-text review.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in human participants (38 males) and reports task-related neural responses in emotion-regulation networks during virtual violent actions. It is unclear from the abstract whether participants were explicitly instructed to regulate their emotions (I2 not clearly demonstrated), so full-text is needed to confirm. I1, I3, and I4 are met based on the abstract; no exclusion criteria appear to apply.

Excluded because the study used olfactory (odor) stimuli rather than the visual-stimuli required by this meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Exclusion criteria met: none (E1, E2 not applicable). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: does not meet the meta-analysis' stimulus-modality requirement (visual stimuli).

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI (I1); participants performed an implicit emotion regulation task (I2); includes clinical SAD group and healthy controls reported separately (I3); reports task-related brain activation/connectivity results (PPI amygdala-vmPFC) and pre/post treatment changes (I4). No exclusion criteria are met based on abstract.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants with patient and control groups), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria NOT met: I2 — the study used a Monetary Incentive Delay task assessing reward/punishment processing, not an emotion-regulation task (no reappraisal/acceptance/instruction to regulate emotions).

This is a structural MRI/DTI study comparing gray matter volume and FA in children; it is NOT a task-based fMRI study and does not report task-related activation or any emotion regulation task. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion IDs not met: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I2 (no emotion-regulation task), I4 (no task-related brain activation results).

Abstract reports an fMRI study of older adults with amnestic MCI addressing affective regulation and frontal dysfunction, but does not specify a task-based emotion regulation paradigm or task-related activation results. Insufficient detail to confirm I1, I2, and I4 from the abstract alone, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI with human participants (BPD patients and controls) reporting task-related brain activation/connectivity during viewing of negative vs neutral pictures with heat pain. Fits review objective (regulate or view without regulating). Abstract does not clearly state participants performed an explicit emotion regulation instruction (I2 unclear), so full-text review needed to confirm. Includes I1, I3, I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Randomized, placebo-controlled task-based fMRI in human participants assessing distraction as an emotion regulation strategy in PTSD patients and controls; reports task-related brain activation and functional connectivity results (thalamus, striatum, amygdala). Thus it meets I1–I4 and no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI with human adults using instructed emotion regulation (increase/decrease negative responses) during a task; reports ACC activation and connectivity related to errors (task-related brain activation). Fits inclusion criteria I1-I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Study is excluded because it does not address the review objective: participants regulated emotion during autobiographical memory recall rather than in response to visual stimuli. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation via cognitive reappraisal), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related activation). No exclusion criteria met (none).

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study where human participants used cognitive reappraisal to up- and downregulate emotional responses to visual threat-related stimuli; reports task-related brain activation (amygdala, prefrontal regions) and physiological/self-report measures. No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract lacks key details: it does not state whether task-based fMRI was used, whether participants performed an explicit emotion regulation task, or whether task-related brain activation results are reported. Because inclusion cannot be determined from the abstract alone, include for full-text review to assess I1–I4.

Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI (I1), an implicit emotion-regulation/emotion-label task (I2), human adolescent participants (I3), and reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results (I4). No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based human fMRI study where smokers viewed emotionally evocative anti-smoking messages; reports task-related activations (amygdala, vmPFC) and a regulation-related brain pattern moderating responses. Fits I1 (task fMRI), I2 (viewing/regulating emotional stimuli), I3 (human participants), and I4 (task-related activation results). No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract investigates neural correlates of emotion regulation in BPD with patient and control groups, satisfying I3. The abstract does not explicitly state task-based fMRI (I1), that participants performed a defined emotion-regulation task (I2), or that task-related brain activation results are reported (I4). No exclusion criteria are met. Insufficient detail to determine inclusion from abstract alone, so include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI in healthy humans (n=18) using an emotion regulation task (reappraisal) and reporting task-related activations (vmPFC, amygdala). Abstract does not specify whether emotional stimuli were visual, so insufficient information to confirm the review's visual-stimulus requirement; include for full-text review to determine stimulus modality. No exclusion criteria met.

Study addresses emotion circuitry and regulation in human first-degree relatives but abstract does not specify whether a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation (view vs regulate) paradigm was used or whether task-related activation results are reported. Insufficient information to confirm I1, I2, and I4, but I3 (human participants) is met. Include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in humans (12 females, 12 males) performing emotion regulation (view vs regulate emotional responses to pictures) and reports task-related brain activation results. All inclusion criteria I1–I4 are met; no exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review.

Task-based fMRI in 40 healthy human participants viewing emotion-eliciting images while applying emotion regulation strategies (goal vs. implementation intentions). Abstract reports task-related brain activation (prefrontal regions, amygdala, OFC coupling). Meets inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria are met or suggested by the abstract.

Task-based fMRI study in human participants (spider-phobic patients) using cognitive reappraisal as an emotion regulation strategy and reporting fMRI activation related to regulation; fits I1–I4. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract. Include for full-text review to extract task-related activation details.

Abstract indicates a neuroimaging study of emotional cue processing but does not specify task-based fMRI, whether participants performed an emotion-regulation or passive viewing task, or report task-related activation results. Exclusion based on failure to meet inclusion criteria: Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical participants). Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study with human participants (45 women) who performed explicit reappraisal and an implicit placebo regulation while viewing disgusting visual stimuli; reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results. Task-based fMRI study in humans reporting task-related brain activation during anticipation of emotional visual stimuli. Task-based fMRI with human participants performing an emotion regulation task (up-regulation of positive emotions to visual images), healthy sample, and reports task-related brain activation (ventral striatum). No exclusion criteria met in abstract.

Abstract provides insufficient methodological detail to determine whether this is a task-based fMRI study reporting task-related activation during an emotion regulation task. Abstract indicates an empirical task-based fMRI study examining emotional reactivity and regulation in generalized anxiety disorder, reporting frontolimbic (prefrontal and amygdala) engagement. Include for full-text review to confirm methods and control group details.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using effortful affective reappraisal (downregulation of negative affect), includes depressed and nondepressed human groups with separate control comparisons, and reports task-related activation and connectivity results relevant to emotion regulation.

No exclusion criteria met (E1/E2: none). Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study with human participants that includes an explicit emotion regulation task (reappraisal) and reports brain activation results; no exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive emotion regulation (positive reappraisal) in human participants; reports task-related activation in ventral striatum, vmPFC, amygdala and connectivity results. No exclusion criteria appear to be met from the abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in human participants (women) reporting task-related neural activation (satisfies I1, I3, I4). Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study (I1) with human participants (I3) and reports task-related activations (I4), but does not describe an emotion regulation instruction or strategy; participants appear to passively process negative vs neutral faces. Task-based fMRI using an emotional faces paradigm (viewing emotional stimuli without regulation is allowed by review). Human clinical older adult sample (late-life depression). Reports task-related functional activation. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI with human adolescent participants and task-related brain activation are clearly reported (I1, I3, I4). Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of human participants performing cognitive emotion regulation (CER) during aversive conditioning and reports task-related ventral striatal and network activation/results. Abstract describes a task-based fMRI emotion regulation study (amygdala neurofeedback during aversive-picture viewing) reporting task-related activation and connectivity, but it does not indicate whether a control group is reported for this clinical BPD sample (I3 not demonstrated). Task-based fMRI study with human participants (24 women) performing cognitive reappraisal/social-distance emotion regulation; reports task-related brain activation (dmPFC, aPCC, amygdala) and peripheral measures. Meets inclusion I1–I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a film-based emotion reactivity and regulation task performed in an MRI scanner, with age-related changes in emotional reactivity and reported brain activation (middle frontal gyrus). Fits task-based fMRI emotion regulation studies; no exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a controlled fMRI study in patients with bipolar disorder, indicating human clinical participants with a control group (I3). Include for full-text review to determine task details and reported activations.

This is a task-based fMRI study with human participants instructed to increase or decrease their affective responses to visual images. The abstract reports task-related brain activation results. All inclusion criteria (I1–I4) are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Excluded because the abstract does not describe an emotion regulation task (I2 not met). No exclusion criteria apply (E1,E2 not met). Task-based fMRI with implicit and explicit emotional-face tasks; reports task-related activation and connectivity; includes clinical and control groups. Addresses review objective (viewing/regulating emotional visual stimuli). No exclusion criteria met.

Study reports resting-state functional connectivity in bipolar disorder, not a task-based fMRI emotion regulation study. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical participants). Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI (I1); uses a cognitive control/'reality checking' emotion regulation strategy during anticipation (I2); healthy human participants (I3); reports task-related brain activation results (I4). No exclusion criteria met; include for full-text review.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study in healthy human participants who viewed and regulated emotional pictures, reports BOLD/neuroimaging results comparing regulation vs viewing. Meets I1–I4; no exclusions apply.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study of emotion regulation in human participants (depressed patients) and reports prefrontal activation predicting symptom trajectory over 6 months, satisfying I1-I4; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports a human trial teaching cognitive reappraisal to alter neural (reward/inhibitory region) responses to high-fat/high-sugar foods, meeting I2 (emotion regulation/cognitive reappraisal) and I3 (human participants). Abstract does not show participants performed an emotion-regulation task (I2). Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in 54 healthy participants, reporting task-related functional connectivity alterations comparing reappraisal versus maintain. All inclusion criteria I1–I4 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI in healthy human participants that manipulates and reduces appetitive/emotional responses to visual food cues via an aversive aftertaste (a regulation-like cognitive control of appetite). Reports task-related brain activation. No exclusion criteria are met.

The study is a task-based fMRI study (I1), with human participants (I3), and reports task-related activations (I4), but it does not involve participants performing an emotion regulation task—it uses an emotional oddball/distraction paradigm without instructions to regulate emotional responses (I2 not met). No exclusion criteria are met (none applicable).

Task-based fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal (emotion regulation) in human participants (psychosis-prone vs low), reporting task-related brain activation and functional connectivity. Fits all inclusion criteria; no exclusion criteria apply.

Task-based fMRI study using emotional (angry/neutral) faces during a working-memory task with patient and control groups; reports task-related functional connectivity differences. Inclusion criteria met: I1, I3, I4. I2 (explicit emotion regulation) not demonstrated in abstract.

Task-based rtfMRI neurofeedback in human participants that involves voluntary self-regulation of emotional (amygdala) activity with positive emotion induction and reports task-related connectivity/activation results; meets inclusion criteria I1–I4. No exclusion criteria met from abstract.

Task-based fMRI with human participants and reported task-related activation, but abstract does not indicate any emotion-regulation instructions. The review accepts studies that view visual stimuli without regulating, so include for full-text review to confirm whether stimuli were passively viewed or regulated.

The abstract describes a task-based (3T fMRI) study using the shifted-attention emotion appraisal task (SEAT), a test of emotional processing and regulation, in human participants given DHEA or placebo, and reports task-related brain activation and connectivity results. Task-based fMRI with adolescent participants and task-related activation reported (I1, I3, I4). Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in human patients performing an emotion regulation task (cognitive reappraisal to down-regulate negative affect), and reports task-related brain activation results. This satisfies inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI of affective anticipation (I1), human combat veterans sample (I3), and neural convergence/task-related results (I4). Include for full-text review to determine whether an explicit emotion-regulation instruction/task was used.

Task-based fMRI study reporting task-related cortical–amygdala coupling during anticipation of a public speech (I1, I4). Task-based fMRI in human participants manipulating incentives to regulate emotional reactions to visual/peer stimuli; reports task-related neural activation differences for regulation of positive vs negative emotions. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (human clinical sample reported). No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion met: I3 (human clinical participants). Inclusion not met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I2 (emotion regulation task), I4 (task-related activation).

Task-based fMRI with adolescents and adults performing directed (emotion judgment) and incidental (age judgment) face processing conditions, providing contrasts that reflect cognitive control of emotion versus passive viewing. Task-based fMRI study with human clinical and control groups (Complicated Grief, Non-Complicated, Nonbereaved) reporting task-related activations. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Task-based fMRI study in human children (ages 8–10) performing voluntary emotion regulation (reappraisal/suppression) of sad film excerpts; reports task-related brain activation loci. No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI study in humans (patients with SAD) where participants performed emotion regulation (reappraisal) of social evaluation and the paper reports task-related brain activation changes; meets I1-I4 and no exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI study investigating emotion regulation in ADHD, matching the review objective. Task-based fMRI study examining neural circuitry supporting emotion regulation using an emotional n-back task in human clinical groups; reports task-related anterior cingulate activation distinguishing bipolar vs unipolar depressed females. Study is a task-based fMRI with human participants instructed to maintain or regulate emotional responses to visual social stimuli (regulation task). Reports task-related brain activation analyses. No exclusion criteria met (not a review; not mere perspective-taking).

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human clinical group), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Excluded because the task is a simple motor response flexibility task rather than an emotion regulation task. Task-based fMRI study in 19 healthy adults that explicitly instructs emotion regulation (cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression) and natural attending; reports task-related brain activation. No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI study reporting cognitive emotion regulation (reappraisal) during scanning in human participants (female sample) with task-related brain activation results (amygdala and prefrontal coupling). No exclusion criteria met and all inclusion criteria are satisfied.

Excluded (E2): This is a task-based fMRI study (I1) with human participants (I3) reporting task-related activations (I4), but it measures mentalizing/perspective-taking without instruction to alter participants' emotional responses—fits exclusion E2; I2 (emotion-regulation task) not met or demonstrated.

Task-based fMRI investigating emotional conflict and reports fronto-limbic activity/connectivity (meets I1 and I4). Task-based fMRI with human participants viewing religious vs nonreligious images during painful stimulation; contemplation of the religious image led to emotional detachment (an emotion-regulation-like process) and the paper reports task-related brain activations (right VLPFC). Study uses resting-state fMRI and examines amygdala functional connectivity in PTSD, not a task-based emotion regulation or viewing task and does not report task-related activations. Inclusion met: I3 (human clinical participants). Inclusion not met: I1, I2, I4. No exclusion criteria met.

Study used resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) rather than a task-based paradigm. It does not involve an emotion-regulation task with visual stimuli or report task-related activation results. It includes human clinical participants (MDD) but fails I1, I2, and I4. No exclusion criteria are met.

Study uses implicit emotional processing (gender judgment) without instructions to regulate emotion. Exclusion IDs met: []. Abstract suggests neural investigation of regulating negative autobiographical memories but does not clearly state task-based fMRI, that participants performed an explicit emotion-regulation task, or that task-related activation results are reported. Task-based fMRI in human participants manipulating perceived control over painful stimuli as a form of cognitive reappraisal/emotion regulation; reports task-related brain activation (dACC, alPFC). Fits broad definition of reappraisal/antecedent-focused regulation. No exclusion criteria met.

No evidence participants were instructed to regulate their emotional responses (e.g., reappraisal/acceptance); task is memory retrieval of painful vs non-painful events. Exclusion: none. Inclusions met: I1, I3, I4. Inclusion not met: I2 (emotion regulation task not demonstrated).

Abstract reports task-based fMRI in a normative human sample and multivoxel pattern results predicting affective valence/arousal (I1, I3, I4). Task-based fMRI in human participants using distancing (a form of cognitive reappraisal) to downregulate emotional responses to visual social stimuli; reports whole-brain task-related activation results (amygdala, PFC, precuneus, etc.). Meets inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apparent.

Task-based fMRI with human participants performing an implicit emotion-regulation task (derogation of attractive alternatives). Reports task-related brain activation results (VLPFC, pDMPFC, ventral striatum). Meets inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria apparent from abstract.

Abstract reports an empirical task-based fMRI study in children performing emotion regulation while viewing emotionally expressive faces and reports task-related ACC activation patterns. This meets inclusion criteria I1–I4; no exclusion criteria apply.

Longitudinal task-based fMRI where adults performed effortful emotion regulation of negative stimuli; reports task-related activation (amygdala, ventrolateral/dorsolateral PFC). Meets I1-I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study where participants (SAD patients) used an instructed emotion-regulation strategy (“reality-checking”) during anticipation and perception of emotional stimuli and reports task-related brain activation results. Task-based fMRI in human participants reporting task-related activations (amygdala/prefrontal). Meets inclusion: task-based fMRI (I1); uses an emotion regulation task (cognitive reappraisal) (I2); human adolescent participants (I3); reports task-related brain activation (amygdala and prefrontal activation) (I4). Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in human (BPD) participants examining neural correlates of provocation-focused rumination, but does not specify that participants regulated emotional responses to visual stimuli or used standard emotion-regulation instructions (e.g., reappraisal). Abstract reports fMRI analysis comparing DAS and NDAS using Granger causality to study emotional networks but does not specify a task-based emotion-regulation or viewing paradigm, nor report task-related activations. Task-based fMRI in human participants (N=24) instructed to view or decrease emotional responses to pictured stimuli (emotion regulation). Reports task-related brain activation. Abstract reports investigation of behavioral and neural markers of emotion regulation in older adults (human participants), but does not explicitly state it used task-based fMRI, a specific emotion regulation task with visual stimuli, or report task-related activation. Task-based rtfMRI neurofeedback study where human participants performed a sustained emotion regulation task (voluntarily modulating positive/negative states) and task-related brain activation results are reported. Task-based fMRI study in humans where participants were instructed to up- and down-regulate emotional responses to aversive visual scenes (cognitive reappraisal strategies), and the abstract reports task-related brain activation results (prefrontal, amygdala). No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based fMRI study with human participants viewing emotional visual stimuli (high- and low-arousal pictures) without regulation; reports task-related brain activation results. Not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation study: I1 (task-based fMRI) not met, I2 (emotion regulation task) not met, I4 (task-related activations reported) not met. Includes healthy human participants (I3 met). No exclusion criteria (E1,E2) apply.

fMRI task study in adolescents with TBI using an Emotional Go/NoGo paradigm; meets I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human clinical participants), and likely I4 (reports task-related neural results). Exclude: Not a task-based fMRI study (I1 not met); uses VBM and resting-state fMRI only, no emotion-regulation task reported (I2 not met); no task-related activation results (I4 not met). Inclusion met: I3 (human participants). No exclusion criteria (E1/E2) clearly met from abstract.

Task-based fMRI with 20 healthy human participants viewing aversive visual stimuli and reporting task-related BOLD activation. Exclusion because the study is a task-based fMRI study (I1), includes clinical and control groups (I3), and reports task-related activations (I4), but does not involve participants performing an emotion regulation task or being instructed to regulate (I2 not met). Task-based fMRI in depressed patients performing intentional emotion-introspection to down-regulate unpleasant affect, with task-related brain activation reported (amygdala, insula, PFC). Meets all inclusion criteria: task-based fMRI; participants performed effortful emotion regulation (emotional faces n-back assessing voluntary attentional control); includes schizophrenia patients with matched healthy controls reported separately; reports task-related brain activation results. Abstract reports task-based fMRI with human participants and reports task-related brain activation (I1, I3, I4). Abstract reports task-based fMRI in clinical out-patients examining brain activation to emotional facial expressions (meets I1, I3, I4). Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study in human participants performing an emotion regulation task (veterans with PTSD and controls), and reports task-related brain activation results (PFC, SMA changes). Included for full-text review. Abstract reports a human (women with PTSD) neuroimaging study of emotional processing, but it does not specify whether a task-based emotion-regulation paradigm was used, whether task-related activation results are reported, or whether a control group is included. I1, I2, and I4 are not demonstrated in the abstract. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion met: I3 (human clinical sample: youth with ADHD). Not met: I1 (not task-based; study examines intrinsic functional connectivity/resting-state), I2 (no emotion-regulation task reported), I4 (no task-related activation results reported). Therefore excluded from task-based emotion-regulation fMRI meta-analysis.

Excluded: PET meta-analysis of REM sleep, not a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation study. Inclusion met: I3 (human participants). Inclusion not met: I1 (not task-based fMRI), I2 (not an emotion regulation task), I4 (no task-related activation results reported). No exclusion criteria met.

EXCLUDED because the study investigates neural substrates of visual exploration/saccades, not emotion regulation. Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (no emotion regulation task or instructions to amplify/dampen emotional responses).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study using a cognitive reappraisal emotion regulation task in human participants and presents task-related brain activation results (vmPFC tracking of subjective and normative valence). No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI in healthy adult humans reporting task-related brain activation (ACC). The abstract does not specify that participants were instructed to perform an emotion regulation strategy (uncertain whether anticipation counts as regulation), so I2 is not demonstrated from abstract alone; include for full-text review to resolve.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I2 (emotion regulation task) — the study uses an interoceptive breathing-load task and mindfulness training without instructed regulation of emotional responses to visual stimuli, so it does not address the review objective.

No exclusion criteria met. The study is a task-based fMRI study (I1), uses human participants (I3), and reports task-related brain activation results (I4). However participants viewed emotional scenes after a depletion manipulation and were not instructed to regulate their emotional responses; thus I2 (an emotion regulation task) is not demonstrated. Therefore exclude based on failure to meet I2.

Task-based fMRI study where participants regulated their own or another person's emotions (interpersonal emotion regulation). Healthy human sample (n=20) and report task-related brain activations. Does not meet exclusion criteria (not merely perspective-taking without regulation).

No exclusion criteria are met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I2 (emotion regulation task) — abstract describes neural responses to negative facial stimuli but does not indicate participants were instructed to regulate their emotional responses, so it does not meet the emotion-regulation requirement.

E2 met: empathy study assessing spontaneous perception of others' pain without instructions to amplify/dampen emotional responses. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human ASD and control groups), I4 (task-related brain activations reported). Inclusion not met: I2 (no evidence of an emotion-regulation instruction/task).

Abstract reports a task-based whole-brain fMRI study with 55 healthy human participants performing instructed regulation of negative emotion (and viewing without regulating). Task-related activation results are reported (GLM contrasts and task-rest interactions). No exclusion criteria are met.

Task-based fMRI study using an affective face-processing task (likely passive viewing), with social anxiety disorder participants; reports task-related activation (left amygdala) and functional connectivity changes pre/post iCBT. The review accepts both emotion regulation and passive viewing paradigms, so inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study is a task-based fMRI experiment in healthy humans reporting task-related brain activations (I1, I3, I4 met). However, participants voluntarily regulated heart rate (physiological arousal) rather than regulating an emotional response to visual stimuli; the task does not meet the review's emotion-regulation-with-visual-stimuli criterion (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports task-based fMRI in human 4–6-year-old children examining functional brain activity related to emotion regulation. It is unclear whether participants were instructed to explicitly regulate emotions, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.

Excluded because abstract does not describe an emotion regulation task (I2 not met): the study examines decision-induced rationalization without instructions to regulate emotional responses. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human participants), I4 (reports task-related activations). No exclusion criteria met.

Task-based rtfMRI neurofeedback study in human combat veterans performing emotion regulation (positive autobiographical recall); reports task-related brain activation mediators and includes experimental and control groups. No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract does not specify a task-based fMRI emotion-regulation paradigm or report task-related brain activation results, but studies adults (human participants). Insufficient information to determine inclusion, so include for full-text review.

EXCLUDED because inclusion criterion I2 (emotion regulation task) is not met: study uses a Go/No-Go punishment/impulsivity paradigm, not an instructed emotion-regulation (e.g., reappraisal) task. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (human healthy participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). No exclusion criteria (E1,E2) apply.

Abstract describes a task-based fMRI RCT where patients viewed negative images or intentionally down-regulated affect using taught strategies, reports symptom change and normalization of brain activation—meeting all inclusion criteria and no exclusions evident.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I3 (human clinical sample with control group).
